drills.q: What must you sort intervals by before merging, and why is that step non-negotiable?
drills.a: Sort by start value. Without sorting, overlap can't be checked in a single forward pass because a later-appearing interval in the input might need to merge with an earlier one that's already been closed out.

drills.q: You're merging [1,10] with the next sorted interval [2,3]. What does the merged block become, and what mistake produces [2,3] as the wrong answer instead?
drills.a: It stays [1,10]. The mistake is overwriting merged.end with the next interval's end instead of taking max(merged.end, next.end); [2,3] is fully nested inside [1,10] so a naive overwrite shrinks the block incorrectly.

drills.q: Prove that once intervals are sorted by start, a single forward sweep is sufficient -- you never need to reopen a merged block that was already closed.
drills.a: If interval k (sorted by start) does not overlap the current merged block, that means start[k] > merged.end. Every subsequent interval k+1, k+2, ... has start >= start[k] (sorted order), so their starts also exceed merged.end -- none of them can overlap the already-closed block either. The block is safe to close permanently.

drills.q: Why does Non-Overlapping Intervals (LC435) require sorting by END time instead of start, and what goes wrong if you sort by start?
drills.a: The greedy 'always keep the earliest-ending compatible interval' is provably optimal via an exchange argument only when processing intervals in end-time order -- keeping the interval that frees up the timeline soonest maximizes room for future intervals. Sorting by start can select a long early-starting interval first, which may block several short intervals that would otherwise all have fit, producing a smaller (wrong) kept-set.

drills.q: Design the min-heap solution for Meeting Rooms II and explain exactly when you pop versus push.
drills.a: Sort meetings by start time. Maintain a min-heap of end times for currently 'active' (room-occupying) meetings. For each meeting in start order: first pop-while the heap's minimum end time is <= the current meeting's start (that room has freed up by the time this meeting begins), then push the current meeting's end time onto the heap. The heap's maximum size reached across the whole sweep is the minimum number of rooms needed.

drills.q: A candidate solves Insert Interval by appending the new interval to the array and rerunning their O(n log n) Merge Intervals solution. Is this correct, and what's the better approach?
drills.a: It's correct but wasteful: it throws away the fact that the array was already sorted and merged, paying O(n log n) for a re-sort that isn't needed. The O(n) approach does a single linear scan in three phases: copy every interval that ends strictly before the new interval starts, absorb every interval that overlaps the new interval by expanding the new interval's own start/end bounds, then copy the remaining intervals unchanged.

drills.q: Why is Interval List Intersections (LC986) solved with two pointers across two separate lists rather than a single merge pass, and what's the rule for advancing pointers?
drills.a: The two input lists are already individually sorted and non-overlapping within themselves, but they represent two different sets that need pairwise intersection, not a union-merge. At each step compute [max(a.start,b.start), min(a.end,b.end)] and emit it if valid (start <= end); then advance whichever of the two current intervals has the smaller end value, since that interval is now fully exhausted against everything remaining in the other list (both lists proceed in increasing start order).

drills.q: A production calendar system re-sorts and re-merges its entire interval set on every single new booking insertion. At what scale does this become a real problem, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Re-sorting and re-merging from scratch costs O(n log n) per insertion; across n insertions total this is O(n^2 log n), which becomes noticeably slow once n reaches roughly the low thousands of bookings processed interactively (e.g. tens of milliseconds becoming full seconds). The fix is a balanced-BST-backed structure (Java TreeMap, Python SortedList, or a custom self-balancing tree) holding the current disjoint merged intervals, where each new booking only needs to check and merge with its immediate left/right neighbors -- an operation close to O(log n) for the lookup plus O(k) for any local coalescing, not a full re-scan.
